deep.reconstruction:
NOTATION (from the previous pages). Gauss writes p t = Σ_n e^{-π n² t}, q t = Σ_n (-1)^n e^{-π n² t}, r t = Σ_n e^{-π (n+1/2)² t}. With τ = i t these are θ3(τ), θ4(τ), θ2(τ). The previous page used p(t+2i) = p t, p(1/t) = √t · p t, and p(t+i) = q t.

PART 1. Modular transformation of p, q, r.
(a) Take integers α, β, γ, δ with αδ − βγ = 1 and set N = (αM − βi)/(δ + γMi).
(b) In τ-language, with τ = iM and τ' = iN, this is τ' = (ατ + β)/(γτ + δ). So N is the image of M under a general element of SL2(Z).
(c) Gauss's side remark (top right) links this to forms of determinant −1 (ac = bb + 1, AC = BB + 1).
   - If M = (1 + bi)/a, then τ = (−b + i)/a is a root of aτ² + 2bτ + c = 0.
   - If N = (1 + Bi)/A, then the form (a, b, c) passes into (A, B, C) by the substitution x = δx' − βy', y = −γx' + αy'. That substitution has matrix [[δ, −β], [−γ, α]], which is the inverse of [[α, β], [γ, δ]]. This is correct.
(d) Gauss then splits into the six residue classes of (α, β, γ, δ) mod 2. These are the six cosets of Γ(2) in SL2(Z), a group isomorphic to S3.
(e) In each class he gives which of p, q, r at M corresponds to p, q, r at N. The multiplier is h = i^α √(δ + γMi), i.e. a root of unity times √(γτ + δ).

Table (columns are cases 1–6):
- hpN = pM, qM, rM, qM, rM, pM
- hqN = qM, pM, pM, rM, pM, rM
- hrN = rM, rM, qM, pM, qM, qM

What these cases are:
- Case 1 is Γ(2) itself: the identity permutation.
- Case 2 is T, τ → τ + 1: swaps p and q.
- Case 6 is S, τ → −1/τ: swaps q and r.
- Case 4 is ST and case 5 is TS: the two 3-cycles.
- Case 3 ≡ [[1,0],[1,1]], i.e. τ → τ/(τ + 1), should be the remaining transposition: p ↔ r with q fixed (see errors).

PART 2. 'Reduction of pM, qM, rM to the simplest form'.
(a) Let M = (α + βi)/(δ − γi), with numerator and denominator coprime.
(b) Set A = α² + β², B = αγ + βδ, C = γ² + δ².
(c) By Lagrange's identity, AC − B² = (αδ − βγ)². So D = αδ − βγ and the form (A, B, C) has determinant B² − AC = −D².
(d) Rationalising gives M = (D + Bi)/C [my computation]. Gauss later writes (D + Bi)/A, which is the same up to relabelling the form as (C, B, A).
(e) Gauss's instruction: find the reduced form (a, b, c) of determinant −D² equivalent to (A, B, C). Then functions of M reduce to functions of (D + bi)/a. This is the arithmetic version of moving τ into the fundamental domain.
(f) The algorithm is Gauss's chain of adjacent forms (Disquisitiones art. 171ff):
   - M = (D + Bi)/A, with DD + BB = AA' and B + B' = hA';
   - M' = (D + B'i)/A', with DD + B'B' = A'A'' and B' + B'' = h'A'';
   - and so on.
(g) Implicit step [mine]: 1/M = (D − Bi)/A'. Hence M' = hi + 1/M. This is exactly the step 2ei + 1/M = M' of the previous page.
(h) So by p(1/M) = √M · pM and p(t + i) = q t, one gets √M · pM = pM' for even h and qM' for odd h. This is what the next page states.
(i) Composing these steps gives the reduction of θ at an arbitrary rational-coefficient point to θ at the reduced point, with the product of √ factors as multiplier.
errors: Case 3 column of the permutation table is wrong. It is identical to case 5 (rM, pM, qM), which is impossible because the six cosets give six distinct permutations. For τ → τ/(τ+1) (α=1, β=0, γ=1, δ=1), θ4 is invariant, since T^{-1}ST ≡ [[1,0],[1,1]] mod 2. The column should read hpN = rM, hqN = qM, hrN = pM.

Placement and form of the multiplier: with h = √(δ+γMi) the correct relation is pN ≈ (root of unity)·h·(θ)M, not h·pN = (θ)M. Check on case 6 (N = 1/M): p(1/M) = √M·pM, whereas h·pN would be √(±iM)·√M·pM. The root-of-unity factor is in general an eighth root of unity, not simply i^α. For case 6 one needs √i while i^α = 1.
'(αδ−βγ)² = √(AC−BB) = D' is a slip: it should be (αδ−βγ)² = AC−BB, i.e. D = αδ−βγ.
With Gauss's definitions, M = (α+βi)/(δ−γi) equals (D+Bi)/C, not (D+Bi)/A as used in the algorithm. This is harmless up to relabelling, since (A,B,C) ~ (C,−B,A).

results.what: Transformation of the three theta-constants p, q, r (θ3, θ4, θ2) under a general element of SL2(Z). Classified by the 6 residue classes mod 2 (SL2(Z)/Γ(2) ≅ S3, acting by permutations of θ2, θ3, θ4), with multiplier ∝ √(γτ+δ).
results.modern_name: Modular transformation law of Jacobi theta-constants; theta group and Γ(2)
results.usually_credited_to: Jacobi (1828–29), Hermite (1858) for the full multiplier; Gauss's Nachlass (Werke III, 1866) contains the p, q, r version

results.what: Dictionary between substitution of forms (a,b,c) → (A,B,C) and the Möbius map M → N acting on the root point (1+bi)/a
results.modern_name: Correspondence between binary quadratic forms and points of the upper half-plane (Heegner/CM points), SL2(Z)-action
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Nachlass, fundamental domain), Dirichlet, Dedekind (1877), Klein

results.what: Reducing theta values at an algebraic point via reduction of the associated positive form of determinant −D² by the chain of adjacent forms (M' = hi + 1/M).
results.modern_name: Reduction to the fundamental domain via the continued-fraction / adjacent-form algorithm; computing theta at CM points
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (DA reduction); its use for theta functions appears in Gauss's Nachlass, later Hermite and Kronecker

results.what: AC − B² = (αδ − βγ)² for A = α²+β², B = αγ+βδ, C = γ²+δ²

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's p, q, r theta notes, including their modular transformations and the link to reduction of forms and the fundamental domain, are known from his Nachlass (Werke III and VIII). This page is a systematic but known-type statement: the six mod-2 cases and the reduction algorithm. It is notable as a clean table, but not new attribution.

checkable.asserts: M' = hi + 1/M in the adjacent-form algorithm

checkable.asserts: Case 3 (τ→τ/(τ+1)): q is mapped to q, i.e. θ4 is fixed (correcting Gauss's table)

checkable.asserts: Case 3: p(N) corresponds to r(M), i.e. θ3 ↔ θ2

checkable.asserts: Case 5 (α=1,β=1,γ=1,δ=0): p(N) ~ r(M), as in Gauss's column 5
